questions.stem: What does a galvanic cell do?
options: It converts heat directly into electrical energy using metals
It produces electrical energy from a spontaneous redox reaction
It uses electrical energy to drive a non-spontaneous redox reaction
It produces electrical energy from a neutralisation reaction
questions.explanation: In a galvanic cell the oxidation and reduction halves of a spontaneous reaction happen at separate electrodes, so electrons flow through an external circuit. Using electricity to drive a reaction describes an electrolytic cell.

questions.stem: In a galvanic cell, which process occurs at the anode?
options: Reduction
Neutralisation
Precipitation
Oxidation
questions.explanation: Oxidation, the loss of electrons, always occurs at the anode, and reduction at the cathode.

questions.stem: What are the charges on the electrodes of a galvanic cell?
options: The anode is positive and the cathode is negative
Both electrodes are negative while current flows
Both electrodes are neutral while current flows
The anode is negative and the cathode is positive
questions.explanation: Oxidation at the anode releases electrons, giving it a surplus and a negative charge. The cathode, where electrons are taken up by reduction, is positive.

questions.stem: Why must the oxidising and reducing agents be kept in separate half-cells in a galvanic cell?
options: If they touched, no reaction could occur because the reactants would be diluted
If they touched, the reaction would reverse and absorb energy from the surroundings
If they touched, the metal electrodes would dissolve in the salt bridge solution
If they touched, electrons would transfer directly and the energy would be released as heat
questions.explanation: Zinc placed in copper(II) sulfate solution reacts, but the electrons pass straight to the Cu²⁺ ions and the solution just warms. Separating the halves forces the electrons through an external circuit, where they can do work.

questions.stem: Two half-cells are joined by a strip of filter paper soaked in potassium nitrate solution. What is the function of this salt bridge?
options: It lets ions move between the half-cells, completing the circuit and keeping each solution neutral
It lets electrons move between the half-cells, completing the circuit through the solutions
It supplies the metal ions that are reduced at the cathode as the cell operates
It stops ions moving between the half-cells, so that the solutions cannot mix
questions.explanation: Without ion movement, positive charge would build up around the anode and negative charge around the cathode, stopping the reaction. Electrons travel only through the external wire, never through the salt bridge.

questions.stem: In a galvanic cell, how is charge carried through the different parts of the circuit?
options: By ions in the external wire, and by electrons in the solutions and salt bridge
By electrons in every part of the circuit, including the salt bridge
By ions in every part of the circuit, including the external wire
By electrons in the external wire, and by ions in the solutions and salt bridge
questions.explanation: Metals conduct by moving electrons, while solutions conduct by moving ions. Free electrons do not travel through aqueous solutions.

questions.stem: In the external circuit of a galvanic cell, which way do electrons flow?
options: From both electrodes to the salt bridge
From the anode to the cathode
From the cathode to the anode
From the salt bridge to both electrodes
questions.explanation: Electrons are released by oxidation at the anode and taken up by reduction at the cathode, so they flow through the wire from anode to cathode. The salt bridge carries ions, not electrons.

questions.stem: A galvanic cell has a zinc electrode in zinc sulfate solution and a copper electrode in copper(II) sulfate solution. Which electrode is the anode?
options: Zinc, because it is the more reactive metal and loses electrons
Copper, because it is the less reactive metal and loses electrons
Zinc, because its ions are reduced more easily than copper ions
Copper, because the copper(II) ions gain electrons at the anode
questions.explanation: Zinc is above copper in the metal activity series, so it loses electrons more easily and is oxidised. Reduction of Cu²⁺ takes place at the copper cathode.

questions.stem: In the zinc-copper galvanic cell, which is the anode half-equation?
options: Zn²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ → Zn(s)
Cu(s) → Cu²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻
Cu²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ → Cu(s)
Zn(s) → Zn²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻
questions.explanation: The anode is where oxidation occurs, and the more reactive zinc is oxidised to Zn²⁺. Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu is the cathode half-equation.

questions.stem: In the zinc-copper galvanic cell, which way do electrons flow?
options: From the zinc electrode to the copper electrode through the salt bridge
From the copper electrode to the zinc electrode through the salt bridge
From the zinc electrode to the copper electrode through the external wire
From the copper electrode to the zinc electrode through the external wire
questions.explanation: Electrons are released by oxidation of zinc at the anode and travel through the wire to the copper cathode, where Cu²⁺ ions take them up. Electrons never pass through the salt bridge.

questions.stem: A zinc-copper galvanic cell has a salt bridge of potassium nitrate. As the cell operates, which way do the nitrate ions in the salt bridge move?
options: Towards the copper half-cell, where positive Cu²⁺ ions are forming
Towards the zinc half-cell, where they are oxidised at the anode
They stay in the salt bridge, because only cations can move
Towards the zinc half-cell, where positive Zn²⁺ ions are forming
questions.explanation: Oxidation adds Zn²⁺ ions to the anode solution, so anions such as NO₃⁻ move towards it to balance the charge. K⁺ ions move towards the cathode, where Cu²⁺ ions are being removed.

questions.stem: A zinc-copper galvanic cell runs for several hours. Which set of observations is expected?
options: Both electrodes lose mass and the blue colour fades
Both electrodes gain mass and the solutions stay unchanged
The zinc loses mass, the copper gains mass and the blue colour fades
The zinc gains mass, the copper loses mass and the blue colour deepens
questions.explanation: Zinc atoms become Zn²⁺ ions, so the zinc electrode is eaten away. Cu²⁺ ions are reduced and deposit as copper on the cathode, and losing Cu²⁺ makes the blue solution paler.

questions.stem: The salt bridge is removed from a working zinc-copper galvanic cell. What happens?
options: The current stops, because ions can no longer move between the half-cells
The current increases, because the half-cells are now fully separated
The current reverses, because electrons now flow back to the zinc
Nothing changes, because the electrons still flow through the wire
questions.explanation: The circuit needs a path for ions as well as for electrons. With no salt bridge, charge would build up in each half-cell at once, so the reaction and the current stop.

questions.stem: Why does a galvanic cell eventually stop producing a current?
options: One of the reactants, such as the anode metal or the ions at the cathode, is used up
The electrons in the external wire are all used up as the cell works
The salt bridge fills with electrons that block the flow of current
The products are oxidised back into the reactants as the cell runs
questions.explanation: A cell's energy comes from its redox reaction, which stops when a reactant runs out. Electrons are not consumed in the wire; they circulate.

questions.stem: A galvanic cell has a magnesium electrode in magnesium sulfate solution and an iron electrode in iron(II) sulfate solution. Which is the cathode half-equation?
options: Fe(s) → Fe²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻
Mg²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ → Mg(s)
Mg(s) → Mg²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻
Fe²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ → Fe(s)
questions.explanation: Magnesium is more reactive than iron, so magnesium is oxidised at the anode and Fe²⁺ ions are reduced at the cathode. Mg → Mg²⁺ + 2e⁻ is the anode half-equation.

questions.stem: A galvanic cell has a copper electrode in copper(II) nitrate solution and a silver electrode in silver nitrate solution. Which is the overall cell reaction?
options: Cu(s) + Ag⁺(aq) → Cu²⁺(aq) + Ag(s)
Cu²⁺(aq) + 2Ag(s) → Cu(s) + 2Ag⁺(aq)
2Cu(s) + Ag⁺(aq) → 2Cu²⁺(aq) + Ag(s)
Cu(s) + 2Ag⁺(aq) → Cu²⁺(aq) + 2Ag(s)
questions.explanation: Copper is more reactive than silver, so copper is oxidised and Ag⁺ is reduced. Copper loses two electrons and each Ag⁺ gains one, so two Ag⁺ are needed. The second equation does not balance charge.

questions.stem: A galvanic cell is drawn with a nickel electrode in Ni²⁺ solution, a silver electrode in Ag⁺ solution, a salt bridge and a voltmeter. Which labelling is correct?
options: Nickel is the negative anode, silver is the positive cathode, and electrons flow from nickel to silver
Silver is the negative anode, nickel is the positive cathode, and electrons flow from silver to nickel
Nickel is the positive anode, silver is the negative cathode, and electrons flow from silver to nickel
Nickel is the negative cathode, silver is the positive anode, and electrons flow from nickel to silver
questions.explanation: Nickel is above silver in the activity series, so it is oxidised: it is the anode and, in a galvanic cell, negative. Electrons flow from the anode to the silver cathode, where Ag⁺ is reduced.

questions.stem: A student makes a cell by pushing a magnesium strip and a copper strip into a lemon and connecting them to a meter. Which statement is correct?
options: Copper is the anode, and electrons flow through the wire from copper to magnesium
Magnesium is the cathode, and electrons flow through the lemon from copper to magnesium
Copper is the cathode, and electrons flow through the lemon from magnesium to copper
Magnesium is the anode, and electrons flow through the wire from magnesium to copper
questions.explanation: Magnesium is much more reactive than copper, so it is oxidised at the anode, and its electrons travel through the external wire to the copper. The lemon juice is the electrolyte, which carries ions, not electrons.

questions.stem: Using the metal activity series, which pair of metals, each in a solution of its own ions, would be expected to give the greatest cell voltage?
options: Copper and silver
Magnesium and copper
Zinc and iron
Iron and lead
questions.explanation: The further apart two metals are in the activity series, the greater the difference in their tendency to lose electrons, and the larger the voltage. Magnesium and copper are far apart; the other pairs are close together.

questions.stem: A galvanic cell has a silver electrode in silver nitrate solution. Why would a salt bridge of sodium chloride be a poor choice?
options: Sodium chloride does not form ions, so it cannot carry any charge
Chloride ions would form a precipitate of silver chloride with the silver ions
Chloride ions would be reduced at the silver electrode instead of the silver ions
Sodium ions would deposit on the silver electrode and stop the reaction
questions.explanation: Silver chloride is insoluble, so Cl⁻ entering the half-cell would remove Ag⁺ ions as a precipitate. Potassium nitrate is often used because its ions form no precipitates and do not react at the electrodes.

questions.stem: A galvanic cell has a zinc electrode in zinc nitrate solution and a lead electrode in lead(II) nitrate solution. Which electrode gains mass as the cell operates?
options: The lead electrode, as lead atoms are oxidised to Pb²⁺ on it
Neither, as both electrodes stay the same mass
The lead electrode, as Pb²⁺ ions are reduced to lead on it
The zinc electrode, as Zn²⁺ ions are reduced to zinc on it
questions.explanation: Zinc is more reactive than lead, so zinc is oxidised at the anode and loses mass. At the lead cathode Pb²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Pb deposits lead, so that electrode gains mass.

questions.stem: What is a battery?
options: A device that converts light energy directly into electrical energy
One or more galvanic cells used as a portable source of electric current
A device that stores electrons in a metal container until they are needed
An electrolytic cell that uses electricity to produce a metal
questions.explanation: Batteries are galvanic cells, often several joined together, that supply current from a spontaneous redox reaction. They store chemical energy, not a supply of electrons.

questions.stem: What is the role of the electrolyte in a battery?
options: It allows ions to move between the electrodes inside the cell
It allows electrons to move between the electrodes inside the cell
It stops all chemical reactions until the battery is connected
It provides the metal that is oxidised at the anode
questions.explanation: The electrolyte, whether a solution or a moist paste, completes the circuit inside the cell by moving ions, just as a salt bridge does. Electrons travel through the external circuit.

questions.stem: Why can some cells be recharged while others cannot?
options: In rechargeable cells the products escape as gases, so fresh reactants can flow back into the cell
In non-rechargeable cells the electrons are used up, so none are left to carry a charging current
In non-rechargeable cells there is no anode, so the reaction can run in only one direction
In rechargeable cells the products stay at the electrodes, so an external current can reverse the reaction
questions.explanation: Recharging uses electrical energy to drive the cell reaction backwards, regenerating the reactants. This works only if the products remain in place, in a form that can react again.

questions.stem: In a zinc-carbon dry cell, which part is oxidised as the cell operates?
options: The carbon rod
The paper separator
The steel cap
The zinc casing
questions.explanation: The zinc case is the anode: Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻. The carbon rod is an inert electrode at the cathode, where manganese dioxide in the paste is reduced.

questions.stem: Why is a zinc-carbon cell described as a 'dry cell'?
options: It must be kept dry, as water stops the redox reaction
Its electrolyte is a moist paste instead of a free-flowing liquid
It contains no water at all, so no ions are present in the cell
Its reaction produces no water, unlike other galvanic cells
questions.explanation: A dry cell still needs mobile ions, so its electrolyte is a damp paste. A paste cannot spill, which makes the cell portable.

questions.stem: Which substance is the electrolyte in an alkaline cell?
options: Ammonium chloride
Sodium chloride
Potassium hydroxide
Sulfuric acid
questions.explanation: Alkaline cells use a paste of potassium hydroxide, a base, which gives the cell its name. Ammonium chloride is the electrolyte of the older zinc-carbon cell, and sulfuric acid is used in lead-acid batteries.

questions.stem: Which description fits a car's lead-acid battery?
options: Lead and lead(IV) oxide electrodes in sulfuric acid; rechargeable
Lead and lead(IV) oxide electrodes in potassium hydroxide; not rechargeable
Zinc and carbon electrodes in sulfuric acid; rechargeable
Lithium and graphite electrodes in sulfuric acid; not rechargeable
questions.explanation: A lead-acid battery has lead and lead(IV) oxide plates in sulfuric acid. The car's alternator recharges it while the engine runs.

questions.stem: A lead-acid battery is discharging. Which change takes place?
options: Hydrogen gas forms at both electrodes and the acid concentration stays constant
Both electrodes become coated with lead(II) sulfate and the acid concentration falls
Both electrodes become coated with lead(IV) oxide and the acid concentration rises
The lead electrode dissolves completely and the acid concentration rises
questions.explanation: On discharge lead is oxidised and lead(IV) oxide is reduced, and both form solid lead(II) sulfate using sulfate ions from the acid. The acid becomes more dilute, so its density shows how charged the battery is.

questions.stem: Which type of battery is commonly used to start petrol and diesel car engines?
options: Alkaline
Silver oxide
Lead-acid
Zinc-carbon
questions.explanation: Lead-acid batteries are cheap, rechargeable and can deliver the large current a starter motor needs. Zinc-carbon, alkaline and silver oxide cells are small and not rechargeable.

questions.stem: Why are lithium-ion batteries used in mobile phones and electric vehicles?
options: They never need recharging, because their reactants are supplied continuously
They contain no flammable materials, so they cannot overheat
They store a lot of energy for their mass and can be recharged many times
They are the cheapest batteries to make and contain no metals
questions.explanation: Lithium is a very light, reactive metal, so lithium-ion cells have a high energy per kilogram, and they are rechargeable. They can overheat and catch fire if damaged or short-circuited.

questions.stem: Why are lead-acid batteries not used to power mobile phones?
options: They cannot supply a current large enough to run a phone
They are not rechargeable, so they would need frequent replacing
They work only at the high temperatures found in car engines
They are very heavy for the amount of energy they store
questions.explanation: Lead is dense, so lead-acid batteries store little energy per kilogram. They suit cars because they are cheap and deliver large currents to the starter motor, where weight matters less.

questions.stem: How does a fuel cell differ from other galvanic cells such as an alkaline cell?
options: Its electrodes are consumed rapidly, so it must be replaced after each use
Its reactants are supplied continuously, so it does not run down or need recharging
It uses electrical energy to drive a non-spontaneous reaction at its electrodes
It produces electricity without any oxidation or reduction taking place
questions.explanation: A fuel cell is a galvanic cell whose reactants, such as hydrogen and oxygen, are fed in from outside, so it runs as long as they are supplied. It still relies on a spontaneous redox reaction.

questions.stem: Why should used batteries be taken to a collection point instead of being put in household rubbish?
options: They are made mainly of paper, which takes up too much space in landfill
They contain metals that can harm the environment and can be recovered by recycling
They contain radioactive materials that must be stored underground for centuries
They become fully charged again in landfill and can produce electric shocks
questions.explanation: Batteries can contain lead, cadmium, nickel, zinc, manganese and lithium. In landfill these can leach into soil and water, and damaged lithium-ion batteries can start fires in rubbish trucks; recycling recovers the metals.

questions.stem: A household installs a battery with its rooftop solar panels. What is the main benefit?
options: The battery allows the house to use electricity without any redox reaction
Electricity generated during the day can be stored and used at night
The battery makes the solar panels generate more electricity in sunlight
The battery turns the panels' heat into extra electrical energy
questions.explanation: Solar panels generate only in daylight, while much household use is in the evening. A rechargeable battery, commonly lithium-ion, charges from surplus solar power and discharges later, reducing the electricity drawn from the grid.

questions.stem: Which is a valid disadvantage of the large-scale use of lithium-ion batteries?
options: They can only be used once, so millions are thrown away after a single charge
Mining the metals they contain can damage environments, and recycling them is complex
They release large amounts of carbon dioxide each time they are discharged
They contain mercury, which escapes into the air while they are in use
questions.explanation: Lithium-ion batteries need metals such as lithium, cobalt and nickel, and mining them has environmental and social costs. Their many components make recycling difficult. They are rechargeable and release no CO₂ when discharged.
